summary: Defines a DHCPv6 option that gives hosts the location of Network Time Protocol (NTPv4) servers. A host can learn which time servers to use automatically when it gets its network configuration. It is a Proposed Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: When you join a network, it hands you a list of things you need. This adds who to ask for the time to that list.

questions: how do hosts discover ntp servers with dhcpv6
what is the dhcpv6 ntp server option
how do hosts find ntp servers with dhcpv6
subtitle: How a DHCPv6 server tells a host which Network Time Protocol servers to use for its clock.

tldr.problem: Hosts that get their network settings from DHCPv6 had no flexible way to learn where their NTP time servers are. The older SNTP option could only carry IPv6 addresses and was not extensible.
tldr.mechanism: A new container option, OPTION_NTP_SERVER (code 56), holds exactly one suboption that gives a server as a unicast IPv6 address, a multicast IPv6 address or an FQDN.
tldr.outcome: Hosts can discover time servers automatically. The RFC also deprecates RFC 4075 and warns that a forged option could skew clocks, so it advises authenticated DHCP or NTP Autokey.

today: RFC 5908 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It deprecates RFC 4075.

sections.title: What the Option Is For
sections.content:
RFC 5908 defines a DHCPv6 option, with suboptions, that gives DHCPv6 hosts the location of Network Time Protocol version 4 (RFC 5905) servers, or a later version. Simple NTP (SNTP, RFC 4330) servers are covered too.

The RFC keeps the option narrow. NTP has many configuration parameters, but the document says changing them is best left to the client, so the option only carries server location.
sections.plainLanguage: The network tells your computer where to ask for the right time. It does not tell the computer how to do the asking, only whom to ask.

sections.title: Usage Model and Responsible Use
sections.content:
Public NTP servers are offered by a number of organizations, and the RFC says they can be used but should not be abused. Any method that spreads NTP server locations must not overload public servers. If a device ships with a hardcoded configuration, that configuration MUST NOT name a server outside the organization that distributes the device. Typical use is an NTP server run by the same organization as the DHCPv6 server.

Because DHCP serves many devices at once, mistakes are amplified. Naming the server by FQDN adds a level of indirection: if the setting is wrong, DNS can point misconfigured clients at an IPv6 address that no host uses, rather than having to change the NTP server's own address.
sections.plainLanguage: Do not send everyone to a stranger's clock, because it could get swamped. Using a name instead of a number lets you fix a mistake in one place.

sections.title: The NTP Server Option
sections.content:
OPTION_NTP_SERVER has option code 56. It is a container with no value of its own: it holds suboptions, and it MUST include one, and only one, time source suboption. It describes one NTP or SNTP server and may appear several times in a DHCPv6 message. Each instance is a server the client should add to its configuration. The option-len field is the total length of the included suboptions.

If the location is a multicast address, the client SHOULD use it as an NTP multicast group and listen for messages sent to it. The RFC sets no priority between a client's own configured servers and those learned through DHCP, and the client may use both at once.
sections.plainLanguage: The option is a small envelope with one note inside. The note says either a number, a group address or a name for a time server.

sections.title: The Three Suboptions
sections.content:
Three time source suboptions are defined, and more may be added later.

  • NTP_SUBOPTION_SRV_ADDR (1): the IPv6 unicast address of a server; suboption-len is 16.
  • NTP_SUBOPTION_MC_ADDR (2): the IPv6 multicast group address NTP uses on the local network; suboption-len is 16.
  • NTP_SUBOPTION_SRV_FQDN (3): the fully qualified domain name of the server. It MUST be encoded as described in RFC 3315, Section 8, and internationalized domain names are not allowed.

The RFC says the FQDN form offers the most flexibility, resiliency and security, while the address forms exist for cases where depending on DNS is not desirable.
sections.plainLanguage: You can give the time server's street address, a party-line everyone listens on, or just its name. The name is the easiest to change later.

sections.title: Where the Option Appears
sections.content:
The order of multiple OPTION_NTP_SERVER options does not matter. The client uses its usual algorithms to choose which servers or multicast groups to prefer.

The option MUST NOT appear in messages other than Solicit, Advertise, Request, Renew, Rebind, Information-Request and Reply. A receiver MUST ignore it in any other message. A client MAY list the option number in an Option Request option in Solicit, Request, Renew, Rebind, Information-Request and Reconfigure messages. If it shows up in an Option Request elsewhere, the receiver SHOULD ignore it.
sections.plainLanguage: There are only certain moments in the DHCPv6 conversation when the time-server note is allowed. If it turns up anywhere else, it is ignored.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
An intruder could use this option to advertise a malicious NTP or SNTP server and damage clients' clocks. The RFC calls the consequences potentially critical because many security protocols rely on time synchronization. For example, an attacker could break connectivity between SEND-enabled nodes (RFC 3971) just by affecting their clocks.

It strongly advises securing use of the option either with NTPv4 Autokey public key authentication (RFC 5906) or with authenticated DHCP as described in RFC 3315, Section 21.
sections.plainLanguage: If a trickster tells your computer to ask the wrong clock, your computer gets confused about the time. Checking who is really talking to you helps stop that.

sections.title: RFC 4075 Deprecation and IANA Actions
sections.content:
This document deprecates RFC 4075, the SNTP configuration option for DHCPv6. The RFC's reasons are that it is not extensible, it causes semantic confusion through the "SNTP" acronym, and it offers only IPv6 addresses, which does not meet NTP needs that also use an FQDN.

IANA assigned option code 56 for OPTION_NTP_SERVER and maintains a new number space of NTP time source suboptions in the BOOTP-DHCP Parameters Registry. Future suboptions are assigned under an "IETF Consensus" policy.
sections.plainLanguage: The old way of doing this was too limited, so it is retired. A new list of allowed note types is kept so new ones can be added carefully.

fields.name: option-len
fields.desc: Total length of the included suboptions.

items.label: NTP_SUBOPTION_SRV_ADDR
items.desc: IPv6 unicast address of an NTP or SNTP server (length 16).

items.label: NTP_SUBOPTION_MC_ADDR
items.desc: IPv6 multicast group address used by NTP on the local network (length 16).

items.label: NTP_SUBOPTION_SRV_FQDN
items.desc: FQDN of an NTP or SNTP server, variable length.
